newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines tiger cub economy begins to mew.
newsitem.headline: Philippines tiger cub economy begins to mew.

text.p: Repeated attacks on the Philippine currency are starting to take their toll on Asia's latest aspiring tiger economy.

But economists and traders said on Tuesday there was enough basic strength in the economy to pull it through and whatever speculators might think, solid growth for the one-time sick man of Asia remained on the cards.
"Our fundamentals are still strong. We can withstand (these speculative attacks)," said Rina Tanhueco, senior associate at the Bankers Association of the Philippines.
The government hopes gross national product will rise at least seven percent this year, though private economists are a little less optimistic.
Monday saw the latest in a wave of speculation against the Philippine peso, compelling the Central Bank to push up overnight interest rates to 30 percent, their highest in 2-1/2 years.
Most view the attacks, triggered by fears that the Philippines was about to suffer the same economic crisis as Thailand, as a temporary phenomenon.
However, it is not without some pain and the peso is not out of the woods yet, they said.

One bank treasurer estimated that as much as $700 million, out of a total of little more than $11 billion at last count, could have been drained from Central Bank reserves in the past two months as it defended the peso.
"How long can it go on? It's got another $1 billion or so (it can afford) to spend," a treasurer at one foreign bank said.
"The spirit may be willing (to protect the peso) but the reserves may not. I wouldn't want to be the central bank right now," he added.
Almost no one expects the peso, whose rate against the dollar has barely changed for more than a year, to take anything remotely resembling a nose-dive.
But it could edge down over the rest of the year, partly in response to exporters who are constantly urging a depreciation to improve their competitiveness.
A stable peso has long been the centre point of Central Bank policy to press down inflation, and one which so far has been successful.
"I see a very stable peso this year," said Hongkong Bank Treasurer Mark Boyne, who thought most of the panickers had already covered their positions.
Also, most foreign investors in the equities markets were not in for the short term and so not likely to go scrambling for dollars every time there were market jitters, he added.

For some, though, it is interest rates -- the Central Bank's major barricade against attacks on the peso -- that cause the most concern and which could hit economic growth if they are persistently high.
"It could have a potential dampening effect on investment," Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice-president at Philippine TA Securities, said.
Banks were already pushing up the cost of loans and if this was prolonged it would eventually hurt such areas as housing and durable goods, he said.
But the situation is not the same as in Thailand.
The Philippine current account deficit is at worst 4.5 percent of GNP compared to closer to 7.5 percent in Thailand.
And money continued to come in -- around $7 billion a year -- from the 5.5 million Filipinos working overseas, he said.
The trade account is heavily in deficit but the government argues that exports are surging and that much of the imports are capital goods that will later boost output.
There is concern over manufacturing, which has already showed signs of weakening growth that will not be helped by high interest rates.
"We have always said the economy will be in for a slowdown. It's part of a cycle. It's just consolidation," Tanhueco of the Bankers Association said.
